tactics.title: Sentinum: Fabius waits, Decius devotes himself

units.label: Decius: legions V and VI with allies
Fabius: legions I and III with allies
Reserve: L. Scipio and C. Marcius

phases.text: After two days of waiting, the armies formed up on the plain below Sentinum. Livy (10.27) puts the Gauls on the coalition right and the Samnites on the left, so Decius with legions V and VI faced the Gauls and Fabius with I and III faced the Samnites. The Etruscans and Umbrians were absent: Fabius had ordered Fulvius and Postumius to raid the territory of Clusium, and those contingents marched home. Livy thought their presence would have meant a Roman defeat. The consuls had agreed opposite plans: Fabius would fight defensively and let the Samnite and Gallic first rush burn out, Decius would attack.

Decius threw his cavalry at the Gallic horse and drove it back twice. On the second charge the Roman squadrons ran on into the enemy infantry and were struck by something new to them: war chariots and carts (essedis carrisque, Livy 10.28) driven in with a roar of wheels and hooves. The horses bolted, the cavalry came back through its own legions, and the Gallic infantry followed up into the disorder. With his wing breaking, Decius called the pontifex M. Livius, recited the formula of devotio dedicating himself and the enemy army to the Earth and the gods of the dead, and rode into the Gallic ranks to his death, as his father had at Veseris in 340.

phases.t: Fabius feeds the left and turns the Samnites
phases.text: Livy says the left recovered once Decius was dead: Livius took command and the troops collected the javelins littering the ground and showered the Gauls, who had locked their shields into a testudo. Fabius, told of the crisis, sent his reserve under L. Cornelius Scipio and C. Marcius across to the left. On his own wing the Samnites were now tiring, so he ordered the cavalry round the Samnite flank and the infantry forward. Losses show where the battle had been decided: Livy gives 7,000 dead in Decius' army and 1,700 in Fabius'.

phases.t: Samnite flight, the testudo broken, the camp stormed
phases.text: The Samnites broke and streamed back past the flank of the Gauls towards their camp. Fabius sent the 500 Campanian horse round the Gallic rear with the principes of legion III behind them, and the testudo, hit front and back, came apart. Fabius himself pressed on to the Samnite camp, where Gellius Egnatius was killed fighting at the gate. Livy's totals are 25,000 enemy dead and 8,000 captured against 8,700 Romans. He also notes, and rejects, writers who inflated the enemy to 60,000 foot, 40,000 horse and 1,000 chariots.

tactics.note: Reconstruction after Livy 10.27-30, the only narrative. The site in the basin below Sassoferrato is conventional, not proven. Unit frontages, the reserve's position and the routes of the flanking cavalry are schematic; Livy's casualty figures probably derive from annalists and are not reliable in detail.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005)

tactics.title: Heraclea: the legions meet the phalanx and the elephants

phases.text: Pyrrhus had camped on the plain between Pandosia and Heraclea, hoping to delay until his Italian allies arrived, and posted light troops along the Siris. The consul P. Valerius Laevinus would not wait. Plutarch (Pyrrhus 16) says the infantry crossed at the fords while the cavalry splashed over at many points along the river, so that Pyrrhus' outposts, fearing encirclement, fell back. This is the first time a Roman army met a professional Hellenistic army, and Pyrrhus, watching the orderly crossing, is supposed to have remarked that the barbarians' discipline was not barbarous.

Pyrrhus led his horse guard into the Roman cavalry as it came up the bank, hoping to catch it before the infantry formed, and ordered the phalanx to deploy. The cavalry action was confused and personal: an Italian (Plutarch names Oplacus, a Frentanian) marked the king out and killed his horse, and Pyrrhus exchanged cloak and armour with Megacles, one of his Companions. The Roman cavalry held long enough for the legions to cross and deploy.

Phalanx and legions now fought on the plain north of the river. Plutarch says the struggle swayed seven times. Megacles, wearing the king's cloak, was cut down and his armour paraded, and the rumour that Pyrrhus was dead shook the phalanx until the king rode bareheaded along the line. For the Romans the phalanx's hedge of pikes was new; for Pyrrhus the legion, which fought in small units and could replace tired men from the rear lines, was new. Neither side broke.

Pyrrhus then brought his 20 elephants round against the Roman cavalry, whose horses would not face beasts they had never seen. The cavalry broke and fled into its own infantry, and Pyrrhus launched the Thessalian horse into the disorder. The Roman army collapsed back over the Siris. Hieronymus of Cardia, Pyrrhus' contemporary, put Roman losses at about 7,000 dead and 1,800 captured and Pyrrhus' at about 4,000; Dionysius gives 15,000 and 13,000. Pyrrhus had lost many of his best officers and men, which could not be replaced from Epirus.

tactics.note: Reconstruction after Plutarch, who drew on Hieronymus of Cardia and Pyrrhus' memoirs. The exact place on the Siris near Policoro is uncertain, and no source gives Pyrrhus' order of battle; the wing positions of the elephants and Thessalians are inferred from the course of events.

tactics.title: Ausculum: wagons against elephants

units.label: Left: Aetolian and Acarnanian mercenaries, Samnites

phases.t: The second day, on level ground
phases.text: On the first day the armies fought on broken, wooded ground near a river where neither the phalanx nor the elephants could work, and night ended an even fight. Overnight Pyrrhus occupied the rough ground with light troops, so on the second day the battle was fought on the open plain. Dionysius (20.1) gives his line from right to left: Macedonians, Italian mercenaries, Ambraciots, Tarentines with white shields, Bruttians and Lucanians, Thesprotians and Chaonians in the centre, then Aetolian, Acarnanian and Athamanian mercenaries, and Samnites on the left, with cavalry on both wings and elephants and light troops behind them. The Romans had built 300 wagons carrying poles with tridents, scythes and fire-pots to fight the elephants.

The wagons went forward against the place where the elephants had stood, but Pyrrhus had moved them, and his light troops and archers shot down the wagon crews and their oxen. Along the main front the fighting was hard and long. Dionysius says the Roman first legion pushed back the Macedonians and that the Pyrrhic centre, where the Italians stood, gave ground.

phases.t: The Daunian raid on Pyrrhus' camp
phases.text: At this point 4,000 foot and 400 horse of Rome's Daunian allies from Arpi, who had lost their way to the battlefield, came on Pyrrhus' camp from behind and plundered and burned it. Pyrrhus detached some elephants and cavalry against them; the Daunians took refuge on a steep height, and the detachment was then turned against the Roman line.

With the elephants committed against the Roman wing, the line broke and fell back to the camp across the stream. Night ended the fighting. Hieronymus, as preserved by Plutarch (Pyrrhus 21), gave 6,000 Roman and 3,505 Pyrrhic dead, the latter figure taken from the king's own records. Pyrrhus was wounded by a javelin in the arm. His reply to congratulations, that one more such victory would undo him, made this the original Pyrrhic victory. Later Roman tradition (Cicero, Zonaras) claimed that the consul P. Decius Mus devoted himself here as his father and grandfather had done, but this is doubtful.

tactics.note: Order of battle follows Dionysius 20.1, the fullest account, which is fragmentary; Plutarch's version (from Hieronymus) is shorter and differs in emphasis. The location near Ascoli Satriano and the river are approximate, and where exactly the elephants broke the Roman line is not stated. Day 1 is summarised in the first phase rather than drawn.

tactics.title: Beneventum: the failed night march

phases.text: Back from Sicily with a depleted army, Pyrrhus split his forces, sending part to hold the consul L. Cornelius Lentulus in Lucania while he moved against M'. Curius Dentatus near Maleventum before the two consuls could unite. Curius stayed in a fortified camp on strong ground. Plutarch (Pyrrhus 25) says Pyrrhus tried a night march with his best troops and the strongest elephants over the wooded heights, to fall on the Roman camp from above at dawn. The march went wrong: the torches burned out, the column lost its way in the thickets, and it arrived on the heights in daylight, exhausted.

Curius led his men out of the camp against the tired troops descending from the heights and routed them. Dionysius and Plutarch say some of the elephants were captured. This first success gave the Romans confidence to come down into the plain and offer battle to the rest of Pyrrhus' army.

phases.t: Battle in the plain: elephants drive back a wing
phases.text: On level ground Pyrrhus' phalanx and elephants had the better of it on one wing, which was driven back towards the Roman camp. Plutarch says Curius then called up the guards left at the camp, fresh men posted on the rampart.

phases.t: Missiles from the rampart and the wounded calf
phases.text: The camp guards showered the elephants with javelins at close range. Dionysius and Florus tell of a calf wounded in the head whose mother turned back to it, throwing the other beasts into confusion; they ran back through Pyrrhus' own lines. The phalanx broke. Two elephants were killed and eight captured, and four of them were led in Curius' triumph, the first elephants seen in Rome. Pyrrhus left Italy for Epirus later that year, leaving a garrison in Tarentum.

tactics.note: The sources are thin and partly anecdotal. The camp, the heights and the route of the night march are inferred; the sequence of a night-march failure followed by a pitched battle follows Plutarch, with the elephant calf from Dionysius and Florus. Some modern scholars think the 'battle' was little more than the defeat of the night column and a wider engagement in which Pyrrhus disengaged.

tactics.title: Mylae: the corvus
tactics.scaleNote: sea area perhaps 6 km across; schematic

phases.text: The new Roman fleet of 100 quinqueremes and 20 triremes had been built in about two months, and its crews trained on benches ashore. Polybius (1.22) says that because the ships were clumsy, someone suggested the corvus: a boarding bridge about 1.2 m wide and 11 m long, hinged on a pole in the bows, with an iron spike underneath that drove into an enemy deck when the bridge was dropped. Hannibal (son of Gisco) brought 130 ships from Panormus. Despising Roman seamanship, the Carthaginians came on bows-first without forming line, expecting easy prizes.

The leading 30 Carthaginian ships rammed or came alongside, and the corvi fell on them. Roman marines ran across and the fight turned into an infantry action on deck, which the Romans won. All 30 ships were taken, including the flagship, a 'seven' that had once been Pyrrhus'. Hannibal escaped in a small boat.

phases.t: The attempt to take them from the flank
phases.text: The rest of the fleet tried to sweep round and strike the Romans on the beam and stern, avoiding the bows. Polybius says the bridges could be swung round in any direction, so wherever the Carthaginians closed they were grappled. They lost more ships, about 50 in all.

The survivors broke off and fled west. Polybius puts the loss at 50 ships; the restored inscription on Duilius' rostral column in the Forum claims 31 captured and 13 sunk, and gold, silver and bronze taken. Duilius got the first naval triumph and the right to be escorted home from dinner by a torch-bearer and a piper. Rome held the sea off northern Sicily for the next four years.

tactics.note: Reconstruction after Polybius 1.22-23. The position of the action off Mylae and the directions of approach (Carthaginians from Panormus to the west, Romans from Messana in the east) are reasonable inferences. Polybius gives no Roman formation. The corvus' dimensions and mechanism are reconstructed from his description and debated (Wallinga 1956).
scholarship: Wallinga, The Boarding-Bridge of the Romans (1956)

tactics.title: Ecnomus: the Roman triangle
tactics.scaleNote: sea area perhaps 15 km across; not to scale

phases.text: Polybius (1.26) gives 330 Roman ships with 140,000 men and 350 Carthaginian ships with 150,000, the largest naval battle of antiquity by numbers engaged if his figures are right. The Romans, heading west along the coast to cross to Africa, sailed in four squadrons: the first and second in a wedge with the two consuls' sixes at the point, the third forming the base of the triangle and towing the horse transports, the fourth (the triarii) in a long line behind, overlapping it on both sides. The Carthaginians formed a single line facing east, with Hanno's right extended far out to sea and the left angled towards the shore.

Hamilcar's plan was to break up the Roman formation. His centre turned and pulled back, and the first and second squadrons, under both consuls, pursued it westward. This split the Roman fleet: the third squadron, slowed by its tows, and the fourth fell behind.

Now three fights went on at once. In the west the consuls engaged Hamilcar's centre. Hanno's right came in from seaward on the triarii, and the Carthaginian left swung round and attacked the third squadron, which cast off the transports and fought. Polybius says the Carthaginians had the advantage in speed, but the corvus made every contact a boarding action, which favoured the Romans.

phases.t: Regulus returns; the inshore wing trapped
phases.text: Hamilcar's centre was beaten and fled. Manlius stayed to secure the prizes while Regulus turned back to help the triarii and the transports. Hanno, seeing him come, broke off and made for the open sea. Regulus and Manlius then pinned the Carthaginian left against the shore, where the third squadron had been holding it, and took 50 ships with their crews. Polybius' totals: 30 Carthaginian ships sunk and 64 captured; 24 Roman ships sunk and none taken.

tactics.note: Reconstruction after Polybius 1.25-28, who probably drew on Philinus and Fabius Pictor. The battle took place off Cape Ecnomus near Licata; Polybius' numbers of ships are accepted by many scholars and the crews by fewer. The geometry of the triangle follows his description; the extent of the Carthaginian line and the exact location of each fight are schematic.
scholarship: Tarn, 'The Fleets of the First Punic War', JHS 27 (1907)

tactics.title: The Bagradas plain: Xanthippus' elephants

phases.text: After the Roman victory at Adys the Carthaginians hired a Spartan mercenary, Xanthippus, who told them their defeats came from fighting in hills where their cavalry and elephants were useless. He drilled the army outside the city and led it onto open level ground. Polybius (1.33) gives his line: about 100 elephants in a single line in front, the citizen phalanx behind them, mercenaries on the right, and the 4,000 cavalry with light troops on both wings. Regulus, with about 15,000 foot and 500 horse, put the velites in front and the legions behind them, deeper and narrower than usual to absorb the elephants, with the cavalry on both wings.

phases.t: Cavalry routed; the Roman left breaks the mercenaries
phases.text: The Carthaginian cavalry, eight times as numerous, swept the Roman horse off both wings. On the Roman left, about 2,000 men, partly to avoid the elephants, charged the mercenaries on the Carthaginian right, routed them and chased them back to their camp. This was the only Roman success of the day, and it took those men out of the battle.

The elephants charged the main Roman body. The velites and front ranks were trampled, though the deep formation held for a time. The Roman troops who pushed through the elephants found the Carthaginian phalanx waiting fresh and in order, and were cut down.

The Carthaginian cavalry, back from the pursuit, closed on the flanks and rear. Polybius says most of the Roman army was trampled by elephants or shot down by cavalry where it stood. About 500 men were captured with Regulus. The 2,000 who had routed the mercenaries escaped to Aspis (Clupea). Carthaginian losses were about 800 mercenaries. Polybius draws the moral that one man's judgment had beaten an army that had seemed invincible days before.

tactics.note: Reconstruction after Polybius 1.33-34. The location on the plain near Tunis is not fixed, and modern labels vary (Tunes, Bagradas). Polybius' account of the wings is clear; the elephant line's frontage and the number of elephants (c. 100) are his figures. The Regulus legend (his embassy, return and torture) belongs to later Roman tradition and is not part of this battle.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957)
